questions.q: Why does this lesson say security and usability are inherently in tension, rather than this being a fixable engineering gap?
options: Because Salesforce has not yet built the technology to make both maximal at once
Because a control that makes unauthorized access harder also makes authorized access at least slightly harder -- that friction is how the control works, not a side effect to be engineered away
Because usability only matters for small organizations, not enterprise ones
Because security controls are always more expensive to license than usability features
questions.explain: A lock that only stopped attackers and never slowed down legitimate users wouldn't function as a lock -- the friction for authorized users is intrinsic to how access controls work, which is exactly why this is a genuine tradeoff.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as Salesforce's baseline security requirement for direct logins to the platform?
options: IP range restriction
Field-level security
Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
A 15-minute idle session timeout
questions.explain: MFA is described as Salesforce's baseline login security requirement -- not optional, though exactly how it's satisfied is still a design choice with its own usability tradeoff.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is one example of a design choice that can reduce friction without reducing security in a specific comparison?
options: Removing MFA entirely for users who complain about it
Using layered permission sets on top of a minimal base profile instead of maintaining many broad, cloned profiles
Granting every user 'View All' and 'Modify All' permissions to avoid support tickets
Disabling session timeouts for all users regardless of role
questions.explain: Permission sets layered onto a minimal base profile let an architect grant exactly what's needed without profile sprawl -- genuinely better than the alternative of bloated, cloned profiles on both the security and usability axes in that specific comparison.

questions.q: Which criterion does this lesson suggest for deciding how much friction a security control is worth in a given organization?
options: Weigh the actual sensitivity of what's being protected and how often users hit the control, against the real cost of a breach versus the real cost of the added friction
Always apply the maximum available security control everywhere, regardless of data sensitivity
Only consider the control's dollar licensing cost, never its effect on users
Apply security controls uniformly without regard to which users or data are affected
questions.explain: The lesson frames the decision as matching the control to what's actually at risk and how often the friction is felt, pricing both the breach cost and the friction cost honestly rather than treating either side as automatically more important.

questions.q: What is 'step-up authentication,' as described in this lesson?
options: A policy requiring every user to re-authenticate on every single page load
Requiring stronger verification only for specific sensitive actions, rather than uniformly on every login
A Salesforce feature that permanently disables MFA after a user's first successful login
Automatically granting 'Modify All' permission once a user passes MFA once
questions.explain: Step-up authentication targets friction where the stakes are highest -- a sensitive action like changing a bank-deposit field -- rather than applying the same heavy verification to every routine login, which is one way to shrink usability cost without giving up protection where it matters most.
